## What is amortization and how does it work? | Fidelity
In an amortizing loan, you pay the same amount according to a payment schedule. Every payment goes toward 2 costs: your principal, which is the amount you borrowed, and interest, which is what the lender charges you for borrowing that money. plan.title: How a Mortgage Really Works for First-Time Buyers
plan.description: A plain-English guide to how a US mortgage works, from down payment and fixed versus adjustable rates to amortization, PMI and closing costs. It also looks at where 30-year mortgage rates stand in November 2026, according to Freddie Mac.

beats.narration: You find a $300,000 home and put just 3% down. So you need $9,000, right? Not even close. At closing, you may need between $14,000 and $24,000 in cash.

props.label: Cash at closing on a $300,000 home with 3% down

beats.chapter: What you actually need to bring to the table

beats.narration: Here is why. A mortgage is a loan backed by the house. The lender is the bank, you are the buyer, and the home is the security if payments stop.
Your down payment is your own share of the price. The loan covers the rest. Think of it as your stake in the house from day one.
Take a conventional loan. With a credit score of at least 620, you can put down 3 percent. On a $300,000 home, that is $9,000 down and $291,000 borrowed.

props.title: Take a conventional loan. With a credit score of

beats.narration: FHA loans are another route. With a credit score of 580 or higher, the minimum down payment is 3.5 percent. On the same home, that is $10,500.
Now the surprise. Closing costs run about 2 to 5 percent of the loan amount. They cover lender fees, title services, the appraisal, and prepaid taxes and insurance.

props.heading: Closing costs: 2% to 5% of the loan

beats.narration: Good news: the lender fees inside that range are the part you can negotiate. Compare quotes, and ask questions before you sign.
One last myth. You do not need 20 percent down. But how much you put down changes your cost, and that is where mortgage insurance comes in.

props.text: You don't need 20% down, but it changes what you pay.

beats.narration: Next comes the rate. A fixed rate never changes for the life of the loan. An adjustable rate, or ARM, is fixed for an initial period, then resets with market rates.
beats.chapter: Rates, amortization and why early payments feel strange

beats.narration: So where are rates now? Freddie Mac's weekly survey had the 30-year fixed at 7.18% on November 5, 7.11% on November 12, a seven-week low, then 7.28% on November 19.
A year earlier, the 30-year average was about 6.26%. The 15-year fixed was 6.66% on November 19, up from 5.54% a year ago.
That gap shows up in your budget. On the loan in our notes, interest alone runs about $684 a month at 7.28%, versus about $616 at 6.26%.

props.label: Interest per month at 7.28%, vs about $616 at 6.26%

beats.narration: Now the strange part. Your payment stays the same every month, but what it buys changes. Early on, most of it is interest. Each month, the principal share grows. That is amortization.

props.definition: Equal payments where each month's interest is charged on the remaining balance, so the principal share grows over time.

beats.narration: Try a $300,000 loan at 7.28% for 30 years. The payment is about $2,053. Month one's interest is the balance times the rate, divided by twelve: about $1,820.
Subtract that from the payment, and only about $233 goes to principal. Your balance falls to roughly $299,767. Almost nothing, after a whole month of paying.
Month two: interest is about $1,819, because the balance barely moved. Month one was $1,820. But principal creeps up every month, and later principal takes over.
That is why early payments feel strange. The payment is steady, but the balance shrinks slowly at first, because interest eats most of each check.

props.text: The payment stays steady, but early on the balance barely moves.

beats.narration: Put less than twenty percent down, and your lender will probably add a charge you never asked for. It's called private mortgage insurance, or PMI. And here's the catch: it protects the lender.

props.definition: Insurance that protects the lender, not the borrower, if payments stop. Typically required with less than 20% down.

beats.chapter: PMI, the hidden costs, and the trade-off to weigh

beats.narration: If the borrower stops paying, the PMI coverage pays the lender back. You still carry the cost every month, but the protection is not yours.
The good news is that PMI can end. Under the Homeowners Protection Act, you can ask to cancel once your balance is scheduled to reach eighty percent of the original value.

props.label: Balance of original value: you can request PMI cancellation

beats.narration: First, send a written request. Second, be current on your payments. Third, expect other conditions, such as having no second lien. Don't wait around, because it won't happen unless you ask.

props.heading: To cancel PMI at 80%
items: Meet other conditions, like no second lien

beats.narration: If you never ask, PMI ends automatically at seventy-eight percent. On a conventional loan, that can mean an extra year or two of premiums. And a new executive order, signed October twenty-second, directs a trial of automatic PMI removal.

events.label: You can request cancellation in writing
Order directs trial of automatic removal

beats.narration: Now the whole picture. Your monthly bill is principal, interest and PMI, plus other homeownership costs. Upfront, you also need cash for the down payment and closing costs, often two to five percent of the loan.

props.heading: The total cost picture
items: Upfront: down payment plus closing costs

beats.narration: Rates keep moving. The thirty-year average was seven point two eight percent in mid-November, up from six point two six a year earlier. Nobody can tell you where it goes next.
So here is the takeaway. A rate is a number that will move. Focus on the monthly payment you can sustain, and the cash you need at closing. This is general information, not financial advice.

props.text: A rate will move. Your sustainable payment and your cash at closing are what you can plan around.

accuracy.reason: Core numbers match the notes and the amortization math is right (payment about $2,053, month-one interest $1,820, principal $233). But the $684 vs $616 'interest' figure belongs to an unspecified loan and does not fit the $300k example, and the closing-cost range is conflated.

coverage.reason: Covers down payment, FHA vs conventional, closing costs, fixed vs ARM, amortization with a worked example, PMI cancellation rules, current rates and a caveat. ARM detail (caps, initial periods) and PMI cost are thin.

structure.reason: Three chapters flow logically, but the opening beats are choppy (beats 3-5 repeat the down-payment point). The $684 figure interrupts the amortization build, and rates sit awkwardly in the middle.

hook_ending.reason: The hook, '$300,000 home... put just 3% down. So you need $9,000, right? Not even close', is strong. The ending takeaway, 'A rate is a number that will move', lands, though the disclaimer ends it flatly.

tone.reason: Conversational, beginner-friendly and clear, with a suitable disclaimer.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary well and the chart and table use real numbers. But beat 1's stat value is truncated ('$14,000-$24,'), beat 4's title is a cut-off sentence, and the beat 22 timeline mixes percentages with a date.

originality.reason: The 3%-down hook and the month-two interest detail are concrete, but most content is standard explainer material. The executive order mention is timely.

instructions.reason: Hits every requested topic with a current-rate date. Length is roughly on target, and the ARM treatment is brief.

language.reason: Fluent and natural. The beat 4 title fragment and a few clipped lines ('Now the surprise.') are minor flaws.
